commenti.body: honestly, i haven't seen Poor Things yet because it hasn't been released digitally (since my country won't react kindly to the movie actually releasing in theatres here)... but the Zulawski comparison here interests me. and indeed, the premise of Poor Things reminds me of Zulawski's Szamanka (1996), which is a brutal (yet ultimately feminist) exploration of patriarchial power dynamics through the destructive sexual relationship between its two main protagonists. spoilers ahead: >!there's also a recurring arc about the discovery of a thousand-year-old shaman mummy murdered by his lover in which the male protagonist had an obsession with, and was ultimately killed in the same manner as the mummy by the female protagonist. the female protagonist also share some similarities with Poor Things' from what i've gathered; both of them don't act "normally" and have this naive, primal qualities that distinguish themselves from the rest of the world.!< if you haven't seen it, i recommend you do!

my not very movie knowledgeable housemate thought it was "steampunk" and I think that moniker doesn't describe all works like it and it came later and I think millenials and gen z are going to redefine everything with this shallow read

The use of fisheye lenses and certain pieces of set / prop design reminded me of Seconds (1966), a film very close to my heart that I'd highly recommend. Also a film about someone undergoing immense physical and mental transformation to achieve a "second chance" at life

German doesn't have large filmography. His most famous works are his last 3 films and they are all stylistically similar. Hard to Be a God being the peak of that aesthetic. If you've seen Hard to Be a God you've got the gist of what his aesthetic is about especially since the reviewer mentioned camera techniques. Same goes for Zulawski, if you've seen Possession you know what's typical for his films like the wide angle lenses, roaming camera etc. Ruiz is different as he has the biggest body of work.

>Are there any specific films from any of those directors you recommend?

German - My Friend Ivan Lapshin and Khrustalyov, My Car! (his best film in my opinion)

Zulawski - Diabel, That Most Important Thing: Love, On the Silver Globe, The Public Woman

Ruiz - City of Pirates, Three Crowns of the Sailor, Mysteries of Lisbon, Three Lives and Only One Death

If you like those check out their other works. With German and Zulawski pretty much everything is worth watching if you're a fan. If not you'll just find them insufferable.

>And what other arthouse films do you feel Lanthimos cribs from?

Not films but Karel Zeman and Peter Greenaway in general.
Won't reveal the spoiler, but I definitely need to see more Zulawski.  *Szamanka*'s plot description alone sounds bonkers and right up my alley.

Forgot to mention it, but yeah, that film came to mind as well.  Curious why Lanthimos was so aggressively employing that perspective: what purpose was he trying to achieve?  I eventually surrendered to it -- I didn't find it annoying nor distracting, per se, but I did wish he cut back on the fisheye lens view even just a bit.
OK, I understand your housemate's thoughts.  So which influences did *you* detect?

Thanks for the thorough response.  I need to see those German films, and I have no idea why I haven't seen more Zulawski films as *Possession* features one of my favorite performances ever by anyone, man or woman.  Thanks for the Ruiz recs: such a large body of work and I wasn't sure where to start exactly, but your suggestions seem like as good as any.  Totally forgot about Greenaway (I guess because I haven't seen a film by him in nearly a decade) but I definitely see that influence; apparently his aesthetic (specifically his symmetrical camera shots) also influenced Wes Anderson.

I would like to object about Herman.

Perhaps among Western viewers, indeed, Herman's last three films are the most famous. And it is clear why they do not correspond to the usual Western narrative about Russia.

But this is not the case in Russia.

If we are talking about movies, and not about the noise about movies, "It's hard to be a god" has been waiting for years and talking about him. When he came out, there was a lot of debate. And then... now he sometimes serves as a reference, how not to shoot the Middle Ages and fantasy. Like, even Herman's is better.

So, I would say Herman's most influential film in Russia is "Twenty Days without War." It had to be removed, even for the sake of one monologue by Petrenko.

Hey there! Well, that's a juicy one to dissect, isn't it? I'm not about to serve up some detailed analysis like a sommelier musing over the hints of elderberry in a fine claret, but here's my two cents.

Lanthimos really has a distinct soupçon of the absurd, so I can see how his work might evoke comparisons to Zulawski's 'Possession'. Especially with that combo of the surreal disjointedness and troubled characters. As for Ruiz, your critic buddy might be thinking of 'The Hypothesis of the Stolen Painting', but again, it's a bit abstract in Zulawski and Ruiz's films.

I reckon the connection to Alexei German might be less about aesthetic similarities (German’s films are generally drearier and less vibrant than Lanthimos', IMO) but more about shared themes of power and manipulation. 'Hard to Be a God' might give you some clues there.

But let's face it, while Lanthimos might have borrowed some techniques, he definitely knows how to sauté them into his unique, quirky blend. So, even if you don't see the direct correlations, don't sweat it!

That said, I always recommend a deep dive into the beautiful madness of these directors. Even if you don't find your answers, you're in for a rare cinematic treat. Just remember: Art isn't maths. These comparisons are just personal perspectives, not indelible watermarks. Enjoy the ride!
You're welcome. As for Greenaway and Andreson I think so too. Drowning by Numbers especially feels like something Anderson would do.
Yes, I was talking more about international audience. I've read that his last 2 films are very divisive in Russia although I also read Lapshin is very acclaimed. Nice to hear native perspective.

Zulawski and Greenaway are my favorite directors and I’ve seen a lot of German and Ruiz and… I think this Jake guy is dropping names of filmmakers he likes more than making real connections. There are potentially hundreds of influences, and these specific three aren’t well known even among cinephiles. Not all directors, even the cinephiles, have the time to dig for obscurities. It’s just a fact of life. We should be glad that we are afforded the opportunity to see these films, but making claims of influence might be a bit much. It’s not as if this is some young director showing his influences on his sleeve. This is a huge shift from his earlier films, but also gradual to some degree. He could have stolen from far worse filmmakers and had the skill to make it reminiscent of our favorites.

If the claim is merely that they use similar techniques… it’s not much of a claim at all. Those guys use every technique you can imagine. But, well, it doesn’t matter much, Jake has won because we’re talking about them.

Great thorough response.  I have a tendency to try and discern the influences of practically any film I watch, not in a conscious effort to diminish the artist's work, or to imply that it's derivative, but to goad me into checking out a work I may not be familiar with previously.

I do this with books too.  Consider this: when I read *Blood Meridian* by Cormac McCarthy during lockdown, I was gobsmacked.  The Faulkner influence is obvious, but after having a discussion with a friend who's also into the same books I am, he noted the influence of *Moby Dick*, which I did not read hitherto.  That finally nudged me into reading Melville's magnum opus, and I could see what my friend was talking about.  (And since then, *Moby Dick* remains one of the greatest books I've ever read.)    

Cormac McCarthy once said books are made of books.   One could also say movies are made of movies.  So when this critic listed the names of three directors who I've heard of but whose works I wasn't very familiar with, it prompted this post, and I wanted to see what movies from these filmmakers users in this forum would suggest, so thanks for suggesting that Ruiz film.

Because quite frankly this wouldn't be the first time Lanthimos has explicitly cribbed from other films.  I remember thinking *Dogtooth* was a fiercely original film when I first saw it, but it would be 14 years later until I watched *The Castle of Purity* earlier this year to see what he was inspired by.  Again, not taking away from Lanthimos or his unique style, but it's always interesting to discover a work you may not have been familiar with previously; see also Bong's *Parasite*, and his acknowledged influence of both *La Ceremonie* and *The Servant,* the latter film I probably wouldn't have watched without Bong mentioning it.

Yeah you bring up great points, and I don't mean to imply that Lanthimos is derivative; he certainly has a unique and idiosyncratic style, and it's refreshing to see that style put to use in a film featuring three famous names, and shown not only in theaters exclusively catering to a niche arthouse audience.

I have a tendency to try and discern the influences of any film (particularly those by auteurs) because in the process, I may end up discovering a film or director I may not have been familiar with previously.  Case in point: Lanthimos's own *Dogtooth*, which I thought at the time was a fiercely original film, but it'd be 14 years later when I finally watched *The Castle of Purity* to see what he was explicitly inspired by.  I wouldn't even have heard of *The Castle of Purity* without reviewers extolling it as the OG *Dogtooth*.

And so when someone like Jake mentions three filmmakers who I'm not really familiar with, it piques my curiosity.  I'd ask him to further elaborate on the connections he sees between the aforementioned filmmakers and *Poor Things*, maybe even suggest some titles by each of them as a starting point, but that would be in vain as he rarely engages with his readers.

But with all of that said, actually we all "win": it prompted this post, engendered discussion, and here we are talking about filmmakers which, as you correctly stated, even a lot of cinephiles aren't familiar with.  

Which films by Zulawski, German, and Ruiz would you recommend to someone who's not really familiar with their work?

I would put Greenaway in there, too: Greenaway is a unique case in that he is a painter who hates the idea of screenplays being based on words - and yet there are few filmmakers that talk more about every conceivable element of filmmaking. I don’t think there’s a better film school than his director commentaries and his lectures. He has an extremely dark sense of humor, but he is hilarious. And his films are extremely dense and dark but can be quite playful. For instance, in A Zed and Two Noughts they tried to light scenes in as many different ways as they could imagine - including by rainbow. Not for the audience, but for themselves. Then there’s the visual counting up from 1-(I don’t know how high) in Drowning By Numbers. And the entire premise of The Falls is essentially a joke. 

As for dark, The Baby of Macon is probably the darkest satire ever made. By a lot.

There are minimalists, and then there is Greenaway. You basically just have to be prepared for excess in every way, whether it be metafiction or nudity or violence or dark humor or playfulness in the midst of the grotesque or opera in the midst of a narrative film or…

For me, Prospero’s Books is among the most amazing and singular films ever made and I would rarely recommend it to anyone, because most people don’t say, “I like my films with a lot of ballet and opera and metafiction and visual metaphors”, but you also don’t have a lot of options if those are your criteria. And The Baby of Macon is incredible in so many ways, but so, so, so dark. The easiest watch might be Drowning by Numbers, but A Zed and Two Noughts also literally sets the stage for his future films by listing their descriptions in a newspaper page. Basically you just have to dive in. Don’t stop at one. Some are better than others, all are more interesting than any normal narrative film. Wes Anderson basically took his style and swapped out the ideas for emotions, although Wes is starting to have an idea or two. That Henry Sugar film was about as close to Greenaway as he may ever get.

Zulawski is a different beast; each film is a bit different. His Prospero’s Books is On the Silver Globe, a sprawling and complex masterpiece unlike anything on the planet, but Diabel is similarly haunting and allegorical. He has straight comedies, like My Nights Are More Beautiful Than Your Days and L’amour Braque, which are amazing. You also have a full-on opera, which is also amazing. Oh, a horror film. You’re not going to like them all, but they’re all in his unique and unrelenting style and those that work for you will amaze you. But you can’t really predict. I was uninterested by his most famous films, blown away by some of his less popular. A true gem. The original guy named my two favorites and another top tier, but also one I don’t care for. But I can’t promise you what you’ll like, it depends on your tastes.

German has distinct periods in his career, and the style of the later films is completely different from the earlier films. I happen to like them both rather equally, but there’s no way to compare. Early period is more realistic and intellectual, later is more frenetic like Zulawski. Both great, just a genius filmmaker.

Ruiz is impossible to describe because he made like 100 films and they’re all different and most are unavailable, and some that are available are… zero budget. But he’s unique, for sure, and his books are excellent. I have seen the ones mentioned above and they’re all good, but I can’t guide you to the other 95.

And if you want a fifth complete oddball, watch a lot of Sokurov. Not just his most famous. He has used every single filmmaking technique in the book, as well. Like Zulawski, it is impossible to feel the same way about all of his films, and that’s not a bad thing.

Right on.  Forever playing catch-up here -- so much films to watch, so little time!  I've seen one Greenaway (*The Cook, The Thief...*) and I'm sure I've seen *Prospero's Books* back in college while taking a Shakespeare course...but *The Baby of Macon* is next on my list, which certainly sounds like the most transgressive film he's made.  I've seen one Sokurov (*Mother and Son*) but I'll definitely look into more of his filmography.

The Cook… has the strongest character of any Greenaway film and distracts from the fun, for me. Not many games in that one. So, so many games in Prospero’s books. So many. The Baby of Macon is filled with games as well, but one game in particular is… more like Squid Game. But, Greenaway is singular and everyone should see multiple of his films, it’s not like you’ll see something like them elsewhere.

Keep in mind with Sokurov that he made an anarchic comedy intercut with stock footage, and it’s exact opposite in Mother and Son. He basically adapts his entire style to whatever film he is making and makes up all of the rules. Some are almost even normal-ish. But the breadth of style is almost unmatched, because he does so much and does each thing so uniquely.

Definitely a lot of Kubrick in his past films like ..Deer as well as Greenaway stylistically and thematically, particularly The Favourite and The Draughtman's Contract [[img](https://zeitgeistfilms.com/userFiles/uploads/films/156/photos/draughtsmanscontract-photo01.jpg)] in which -  *a brash young draftsman, is hired to make 12 landscape illustrations at the estate of Mr. Herbert (Dave Hill) and his wife (Janet Suzman). Aside from monetary compensation, the arrangement includes a sexual liaison offered to Neville by Mrs. Herbert while her estranged husband is away*

A couple of Lanthimos' films have make me think of a stylistic tendency you could call (in an over-educated, Katherine-Hepburn-esqe voice) "post-Bressonian". I've seen it in films by Hal Hartley, Bruno Dumont and in Lanthimos's Dogtooth and The Lobster.
